facts.fact_text: The present case concerns alleged restrictions imposed by the authorities on the exercise of the applicants' freedom of peaceful assembly.
On 5 October 2018 the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 notified the prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow of his intention to hold a picket (пикетирование) on 11 October 2018.
The picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was planned to run from 12 noon to 3 p.m. on 11 October 2018.
The picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was to take place in front of the State Duma (lower chamber of the Russian Parliament) building in central Moscow.
Twenty people were expected to attend the picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19.
The aim of the picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was to protest against the increase in the State pension age recently voted by the State Duma.
On 10 December 2018 the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 notified the Moscow government of their intention to hold a public gathering on 22 December 2018 in Pushkin Square in central Moscow.
The public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 was planned to run from 2 to 5 p.m. on 22 December 2018.
About 1,000 people were expected to attend the public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19.
The aim of the public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 was to mark the anniversary of the first post-war political protest held in Pushkin Square on 5 December 1965.
The aim of the public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 was to urge the authorities to respect rights to freedom of expression and assembly.
On 5 October 2018 a deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow refused to approve the location chosen by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 for the picket.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that the venue chosen by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was unsuitable for public events because it would be impossible to meet safety requirements there.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that holding a picket at the chosen venue might result in disruption to the functioning of public utilities, transport, social or communications services.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that holding a picket at the chosen venue might result in obstruction of pedestrian traffic or a breach of the rights and interests of citizens not participating in the notified event.
The Moscow Department of Regional Security proposed that the applicants' gathering in Application No. 31119/19 be held at a special venue for public events in Sokolniki Park.
The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that the deputy prefect's decision met the requirements of section 8 of the Public Events Act.

The Moscow City Court concluded that the contested decision by the deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow was within its statutory powers, the procedure for adopting it was complied with, there were reasons for adopting the decision, and its content met the applicable statutory requirements.

The Moscow City Court concluded that the contested decision by the Moscow government in Application No. 31119/19 was within its statutory powers, the procedure for its adoption was respected, there were reasons for adopting that decision, and its content met the applicable statutory requirements.
The Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015) entered into force on 15 September 2015.

The Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015) replaced Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure governing the procedure for examining complaints about decisions, acts or omissions of State and municipal authorities and officials.

The Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015) replaced the Judicial Review Act (Law no. 4966-1 of 27 April 1993 on judicial review of decisions and acts violating citizens' rights and freedoms).

Under Article 219 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), a complaint against the authorities' decisions concerning the change of location or time of a public event must be lodged with a court within ten days of the date on which the complainant learnt of the breach of his rights.

Under Article 226 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), complaints against authorities' decisions concerning the change of location or time of a public event must be examined by courts within ten days.

Under Article 226 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), if a complaint is lodged before the planned date of the public event, it must be examined at the latest on the eve of that date.

Under Article 227 §§ 4 and 6 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), a reasoned judicial decision must be prepared as soon as possible on the same day and immediately served on the complainant.
Under Article 227 § 8 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the judicial decision is subject to immediate enforcement.

Under Article 305 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), if an appeal has been lodged against the first-instance decision before the planned date of the public event, it must be examined at the latest on the eve of that date.
Under Article 226 § 8 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), when examining the case, the court must review the lawfulness of the contested decision.

Under Article 226 § 9 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the court must examine whether the State or municipal authority had competence to make the contested decision, whether the procedure prescribed by law for its adoption was respected, whether the contested decision was taken on the grounds prescribed by law, and whether the contents of the contested decision met the requirements of law.
Under Article 226 § 11 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the burden of proof as to the lawfulness of the contested decision lies with the authority concerned.

Under Article 226 § 11 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the complainant has to prove that his rights and freedoms have been breached by the contested decision and that he has complied with the time-limit for lodging the complaint.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that the venue chosen by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was unsuitable for public events because it would be impossible to meet safety requirements there.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that holding a picket at the chosen venue might result in disruption to the functioning of public utilities, transport, social or communications services.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that holding a picket at the chosen venue might result in obstruction of pedestrian traffic or a breach of the rights and interests of citizens not participating in the notified event.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that regional and local law-enforcement authorities have an obligation to ensure public order and safety during public events and should take these circumstances into account when proposing to change the location of a public event.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the law-enforcement authorities complied with the statutory prohibition on putting public order and safety of citizens at risk if holding a public event at the same venue where a popular cultural event has already been approved.

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that public interests justifying a change of location or time may include normal functioning of essential public utilities, social and transport infrastructure and communications; maintenance of public order and safety of citizens; disruption of pedestrians or traffic or of citizens' access to residential premises or to social or transport facilities; and other similar considerations (point 12).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that any restrictions imposed on assemblies must have a formal basis in law and be based on one or more legitimate grounds: national security, public safety, public order, the protection of public health or morals, and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others (paragraph 28).

The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 submitted before the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow that it was crucial to hold the event in front of the State Duma building, as the deputies were there daily.

The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 submitted before the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow that the pedestrian pavement in front of the State Duma building was large enough to allow the picket to take place without obstructing pedestrian traffic or access to the State Duma.
Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 pointed out the importance of holding the event in Pushkin Square, stemming from the fact that the protest of 5 December 1965 had also been held there.

Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 stated that the alternative location proposed by the Moscow Department of Regional Security (Sokolniki Park) was incompatible with the event's purposes as it was too far away from the headquarters of the public authorities targeted by its intended message.
The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 stressed before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow that Pushkin Square was the only venue that would allow the event's purposes to be achieved.

The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 relied before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow on Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018, in particular its requirement that interference be justified through the submission of evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found that the office of the prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow replied that another event had already been planned to take place in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018 from 7.30 a.m. to 8 p.m., namely the 'Moscow Traditions of New Year Celebrations'.

The Moscow City Court found that the celebrations in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018 would occupy 3,000 sq. m, making it impossible to hold the applicants' public event in Application No. 31119/19.

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that courts must examine all the grounds advanced by the public authority and all the evidence submitted by it and assess whether the reasons for the interference were relevant and sufficient (point 9).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that a proposal to change the location or time of a public event or the manner in which it is to be conducted must not be arbitrary or unreasoned, and must mention specific facts showing that public interest considerations make it manifestly impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that inconvenience caused to citizens by a public event or an assumption by the authorities that there might be a risk of such inconvenience may not in themselves be considered valid reasons for changing the location or time of a public event (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the public authority must submit to the court evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time, and courts may not take into account any circumstances which were not mentioned in the proposal to change the location or time of the public event (point 12).

In cases where the authorities' refusals to approve the location and time of the public event were found to be lawful and well-reasoned, first-instance courts scrutinized the reasons behind these decisions, including assessment of potential participant numbers making it impossible to host two events concurrently at one place.

In cases where the authorities' refusals to approve the location and time of the public event were found to be lawful and well-reasoned, first-instance courts scrutinized the reasons behind these decisions, including consideration of construction works planned at the chosen location and time of the event.

In some instances, appellate courts overturned lower courts' decisions, finding that local authorities' refusals to approve public events were not well-reasoned because they lacked reference to specific facts or evidence.

The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) stresses that it is the privilege of the organiser to decide which location fits best, as demonstrations often need to be conducted in certain specific areas in order to attract attention, and that respect for the autonomy of the organizer in deciding on the place of the event should be the norm.

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the principle of proportionality requires that authorities do not routinely impose restrictions which would fundamentally alter the character of an event, such as relocating assemblies to less central areas of a city (paragraph 29).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that restrictions to the right to freedom of peaceful assembly must be both necessary to achieve a legitimate aim and proportionate to such aim, and that the reasons provided by the authorities for any restriction should be relevant and sufficient, convincing and compelling, and based on a comprehensive assessment of the relevant facts (paragraph 131).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the principle of proportionality requires that authorities should generally not impose restrictions which would fundamentally alter the character of an event, such as relocating assemblies to less central areas of a city (paragraph 131).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that at the core of the right to freedom of assembly is the ability of the assembly participants to choose the place where they can best communicate their message to their desired audience, and that it would be disproportionate if authorities categorically excluded places suitable and open to the public as sites for peaceful assemblies (paragraph 147).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the fact that a message could also be expressed in another place is by itself insufficient reason to require an assembly to be held elsewhere, even if that location is within sight and sound of the target audience, and that other means of conveying expression such as placement of video screens are not adequate substitutes for the physical presence of assembly participants within sight and sound of the intended audience (paragraph 147).
The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that the State has a duty to facilitate and protect peaceful assembly.

The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) recommends that a co-operative process between the organizer and the authority be established in order to give the organizer the possibility to improve the framework of the assembly, and that the decision-making and review process be fair and transparent.

The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that the organizer of an assembly should not be compelled or coerced either to accept whatever alternative(s) the authorities propose or to negotiate with the authorities about key aspects, particularly the time or place, of a planned assembly, as to require otherwise would undermine the very essence of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association stated in his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27) that organisers of peaceful assemblies should not be coerced to follow the authorities' suggestions if these would undermine the essence of their right to freedom of peaceful assembly (§ 40 of the Report).

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association warned in his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27) against the practice whereby authorities allow a demonstration to take place only in the outskirts of the city or in a specific square where its impact will be muted (§ 40 of the Report).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that where simultaneous assemblies cannot be facilitated, the organisers should be encouraged to explore alternative options that might yield a mutually satisfactory resolution, and where such a resolution cannot be found, the authorities should still seek to accommodate the different assemblies ensuring that any alternative locations remain within sight and sound of the target audiences (paragraph 78).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that a 'first come, first served' rule must not be implemented in a way that enables some assembly organisers to 'block-book' particular locations, and that simply prohibiting an assembly in the same place and at the same time as an already notified or planned public assembly in cases where both can reasonably be accommodated is likely to amount to a disproportionate and possibly discriminatory response (paragraph 78).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that assemblies should be facilitated within 'sight and sound' of their target audience unless compelling reasons necessitate a change of venue, and that in those cases alternative sites should be provided that are as close as possible to the initially proposed site (paragraph 82).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that involvement in prior negotiations on the part of the organizers should be entirely voluntary, and an unwillingness or refusal to engage in dialogue with the authorities should not have negative repercussions for the organizers or their assembly (paragraph 124).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that those seeking to exercise the right to freedom of peaceful assembly should have recourse to a prompt and effective remedy against decisions disproportionately, arbitrarily or illegally restricting or prohibiting assemblies, and that the relevant court decisions should be issued prior to the planned events (paragraph 125).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that in both administrative and court proceedings, the burden of proof should be on the relevant state authority to prove that the restrictions imposed are justified, and that courts or tribunals should have the authority to review all circumstances of the case (paragraph 125).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the designated public authorities and law enforcement officials should make every effort to reach a mutual agreement with the organizers of an assembly on the time, place, and manner of the event (paragraph 169).
